You're in the middle of something growing and you're not pushing it. That's rarer than it sounds — most care either clutches or lets go too soon. Yours stays in the room and lets the thing find its own shape.

One way to tell it's holding: you give attention without draining yourself, and the thing you tend grows without you standing over it. Keeping that costs something. You notice when holding turns into gripping, and you ease off. Right now you're close enough to help, far enough to let it happen. Trusting the thing to keep going is the part you keep having to practice.
1.sheetLine: You're tending it without forcing it, and that's the whole of it.

2.tense: You are already bracing for a version of this that has not happened yet.
2.verb: tending what needs to grow without forcing the outcome
2.place: becoming what you already are
2.ask: Let one thing move at its own speed today. Say nothing, fix nothing, and see what it does without you.
2.core:
You're standing over something that's growing and bracing for what it might become. Not the thing itself — the version ahead of it. So every check-in turns into a correction, every quiet moment a chance to steer. Nothing is wrong yet, and you're treating it like it's already failing.

When this is working you're close enough to help and far enough to let it breathe. Right now you're close enough that it can't. One day of not steering will tell you more than another week of steering. Waiting is not the same as doing nothing. It's the part of the work that can't be done by you.
2.sheetLine: You're bracing for a future that hasn't happened yet.

3.tense: You stopped offering what you had to give, and that door is already behind you.
3.verb: tending what needs to grow without forcing the outcome
3.place: becoming what you already are
3.ask: Start one small thing you've been putting off, only for yourself. Tell no one. Do it badly, once.
3.core:
There's something in you that knows how to tend, and it isn't tending anything right now. So you call it independence, you call it not needing anyone. But nothing is growing, and you can feel it.

When this is working, you give attention easily and let something small develop on its own schedule without checking whether it's worth your time. The trouble starts when the growing thing would be yours. Pick one small thing — a plant, a page, a habit — and let yourself be bad at it in private, with nobody watching and nobody to report back to. It doesn't need an audience or a result. It just needs you to start.
3.sheetLine: You stopped offering, and you called it independence.

4.tense: You are already the one holding things together, and you did not agree to it.
4.verb: tending what needs to grow without forcing the outcome
4.place: becoming what you already are
4.ask: Name one act of care you've been calling just being practical. Say it out loud to one person.
4.core:
People bring you what they can't carry. You take it, you hold it, you keep the room steady — and you'd describe all of it as just what you do. But nobody asked you to become the caretaker. You slid into it, or it slid onto you, and now it's the shape you're in.

When this is working, you're still the one who holds things, but you know you're doing it, and you choose when to stop. The cost of that balance is claiming the care as yours before you can put any of it down. That release isn't walking away. It's saying: this is what happens, and it's mine to decide. The depletion comes from carrying it without the claim.
4.sheetLine: You're already the caretaker. You just didn't say yes to it.

1.tense: You are looking after something that is growing, and it is not draining you.
1.verb: Tending what needs time to become itself
1.place: Where you see the whole pattern without stepping out of it
1.ask: Pick one thing you're tending and leave it alone for a full day. Notice what it does without you.
1.core:
You can watch the pieces of this fall into place, and you let that set the pace. Your hand goes where a hand actually helps. The parts that don't need you, you let be. People around you can feel the difference between being held and being held down, and with you they feel held, which is why what you tend tends to come along.

Nothing here is asking you for a result. You're not checking on it to see whether it worked. When you catch yourself looking, go back to the ordinary act — watering, waiting, the green that shows up on its own. Growth is not something you produce. Not grabbing is what keeps this from wearing you down.
1.sheetLine: You look after things without holding them down.

2.tense: You are already caring for a version of this that hasn't arrived yet.
2.verb: Tending what needs time to become itself
2.place: Where you see the whole pattern without stepping out of it
2.ask: Ask one person what they actually need from you today. Do only that, even if it feels like not enough.
2.core:
The pieces of a situation come together for you before they come together on their own. You can see which ones are still forming and you let them form. Your attention works a step back, and people bring you more of what's true because you haven't decided in advance what it means.

Right now you're correcting the thing before it has a shape. Your care is running on a schedule the other person didn't agree to — tending a future version of them while they stand here in front of you. That stops being looking after and starts being steering. People feel held too tightly and they stop telling you what's really going on. Stay with the unclear part a while. You don't need the whole road to take the next step.
2.sheetLine: You're caring for a future that isn't here yet.

3.tense: You were tending something of your own, and you set it down and walked off.
3.verb: Tending what needs time to become itself
3.place: Where you see the whole pattern without stepping out of it
3.ask: Pick one small thing you used to enjoy making or growing. Give it fifteen minutes today, no goal, no finish line.
3.core:
Something of your own can sit open on the table with your hands on it. You can read how the parts connect, and that reading points at your own work as easily as it points at anyone else's. There's warmth in it rather than distance, and the thing you tend is allowed to be small and unfinished.

What comes easily is the pattern in other people's lives. Your hands stay off your own. At some point, tending something of your own started to look risky, so the hands came off. What gets called independence is really a door you've been standing at, waiting for a pull that doesn't come while you wait. It comes while you're in contact with what you actually want. Let one small thing matter to you again — not for what it produces, just to feel the draw.
3.sheetLine: You stopped tending your own growth and called it independence.

4.tense: You are the one people hand things to, and you did not choose that.
4.verb: Tending what needs time to become itself
4.place: Where you see the whole pattern without stepping out of it
4.ask: Tell one person plainly what you need from them today. Say it without apologizing for it first.
4.core:
You can see what needs tending in a room and you decide your own part in it. What gets your attention is a choice you're making, not a job that landed on you. The care moves outward and something comes back, and you keep track of which is which because the difference matters to you.

People bring you what needs tending, and you tend it. Somewhere along the line that arrangement set itself up without a decision, and now you're in it, running low in a way nobody around you seems to notice. Not them. Not you. You've been calling it just being practical, just being the one who handles things, and that name has kept the cost off the books. Set one piece of it down. Not walking away. Just putting down something you don't remember picking up, and watching what stays.
4.sheetLine: You're carrying a role you didn't choose and haven't named.

1.tense: The care is steady and it runs on its own supply, not on the other person's response.
1.verb: tend what is still forming
1.place: the table where the finished work gets set down
1.ask: Name one thing you're tending, and say out loud where it's finished. Then let that part be finished. Today, in your own words.
1.core:
What you're looking after is actually getting stronger. You can hold something steady without clamping down on it, and you can wait through the slow part without calling the slow part a failure. That's not patience as a virtue — it's patience as a skill, and it's working.

It works because you let things be done. When something reaches the end of what you can give it, you hand it off, or you let it stand, and you don't keep poking it to prove you're still needed. A good year here looks like things you started that no longer need you. What keeps it: you still have to notice the moment it's done, and that moment is quieter than the urge to keep going.
1.sheetLine: Let the finished thing be finished, and don't take it back up.

2.tense: You are bracing for a version of this that hasn't arrived, and you're writing the ending before anyone else gets to.
2.verb: tend what is still forming
2.place: the table where the finished work gets set down
2.ask: Pick one thing you're managing closely. For one day, do nothing to it — no check, no fix, no nudge — and write down what you wanted to do.
2.core:
Your care has gone past what the thing needs. You're holding the shape of what's coming before it's had a chance to form, steering it away from an outcome you can picture and can't stand. What you give is real. The extra is the grip.

When this is steady, you hold something loosely and it still turns out. You're needed for the conditions, not for every move. In this stretch the person is inside the work, and they can feel you in there. Letting one day go unfixed won't hurt them. It also won't tell you what they need — you'll only find that out by not deciding it first.
2.sheetLine: You're holding it so tight there's no room left for it to grow.

3.tense: You stopped tending at a door you're still standing in front of, and the room is behind you now.
3.verb: tend what is still forming
3.place: the table where the finished work gets set down
3.ask: Do one small piece of care for something of yours — a plant, a page, a meal — and let it be enough for the day.
3.core:
Nothing's growing because nothing's being fed. The care is still there under the surface, but it's pointed inward at staying upright, and staying upright doesn't produce anything. What looks like not needing anyone is mostly the arms staying folded.

The version of this that works doesn't start with a big opening up. It starts with something small you actually want to keep alive, and giving it a little attention without asking it to become anything yet. That's not a mood you wait to find. It's a thing you do, the same size tomorrow, and it builds something you can point at.
3.sheetLine: You folded your arms to stay steady, and nothing gets fed that way.

4.tense: You are already doing the tending, in a room you keep describing as just how things are.
4.verb: tend what is still forming
4.place: the table where the finished work gets set down
4.ask: Find one thing you're carrying that nobody handed you. Say plainly whose it is, then hand it back or put it down, today.
4.core:
People come to you with their weight and you take it, and you talk about it like it just happens. The care runs the whole time — it shapes your week, your mood, what you cancel — and you'd say you're being practical about it. The doing is real. The owning of it isn't there.

When this is steady, you choose what you pick up, and you can set down what isn't yours without it being a betrayal. Nothing about being the one people lean on is wrong. What's off is that it happened without a decision, and the cost lands on you quietly. One small hand-back won't end anything. It'll just show you where the line is.
4.sheetLine: You're carrying a load you didn't agree to, and calling it normal.
